list.listitem: A 5-dose series of acellular pertussis vaccine is recommended for children A, and the tetanus toxoid, reduced diphtheria toxoid, and acellular pertussis (Tdap) booster is recommended once for adolescents at ages 11 to 12 years, and for adults older than 19 years who have never received Tdap. Pregnant women should receive Tdap with each pregnancy, between 27 and 36 weeks gestation.B
Suspect pertussis in patients with cough for more than 2 weeks accompanied by vomiting, apnea, or an inspiratory "whoop." C
If suspected, order polymerase chain reaction (PCR) using a polyester nasopharyngeal swab. C

First-line therapy is a macrolide antibiotic (e.g., azithromycin for 5 days or clarithromycin for 7 days; see ); sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim is an alternative. The overall quality of treatment trials is very limited, though. B

background.definition: Pertussis, also called whooping cough, is a respiratory infection caused by the Bordetella pertussis bacteria and characterized by a prolonged course with frequent paroxysms of cough.

list.listitem: Incidence of hospitalization for pertussis among infants aged less than 1 year is 65/100,000/year based on the Kids' Inpatient Database.

The rate varies with age: 90/100,000 at less than 1 month, 239/100,000 at 1 to 2 months, 77/100,000 at 3 to 4 months, 17/100,000 at 5 to 6 months, and 7/100,000 at 7 to 11 months. The rate in infants has been increasing, from 34/100,000/year infants in the 1980s to 51/100,000/year in the 1990s.
Average annual incidence among adolescents varies by state, and ranges from 11 to 132/100,000/year. Incidence has been increasing in recent years.
Pertussis is much more common in developing countries, with an estimated 20 to 40 million cases annually worldwide.
However, thousands of cases have also been reported in poorly vaccinated regions of the United States and Canada in 2024 and 2025.
Clinically suspected cases of pertussis should be reported to the local Health Department prior to laboratory confirmation.
Bordetella pertussis bacteria.
Bordetella parapertussis, and less commonly, Bordetella bronchiseptica and Bordetella holmesii cause a similar but milder illness.
Bordetella pertussis is a Gram-negative coccobacillus. Toxins released by the organism damage the respiratory epithelium and trigger an inflammatory response, including lymphocytosis.

There is a 7- to 10-day incubation period (can be as few as 5 days or as many as 21 days). The disease can be transmitted via respiratory droplets during approximately the first month of clinical illness. Mild or asymptomatic infections are relatively common in studies of household contacts.
Immunization with diphtheria, tetanus, and acellular pertussis vaccine is recommended at 2, 4, and 6 months, followed by boosters at 15 to 18 months and 4 to 6 years.A

Vaccination with Tdap is recommended for adolescents at ages 11 to 12 years, and for adults in place of the Td booster once if they have not been previously vaccinated with Tdap. For adults, there is no minimum period of time needed between Td and the first Tdap.B
A systematic review found that the multi-component aP vaccine is effective in preventing whooping cough in children, with fewer adverse effects than whole cell vaccines.A
The efficacy of the acellular DTaP vaccine wanes significantly over the 5 years following the final dose.A

Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends that all pregnant women receive Tdap during pregnancy, irrespective of the patient's prior history of receiving Tdap. A large clinical trial evaluated maternal and infant outcomes in approximately 15,000 women who did and did not receive the acellular pertussis component, and found no evidence of harm. Optimal timing for Tdap is between 27 and 36 weeks gestation, though Tdap may be given at any time during pregnancy. For women not previously vaccinated with Tdap, if Tdap is not given during pregnancy, it should be given immediately postpartum. Adolescents and adults who have/anticipate having close contact with an infant <12 months should receive Tdap if not received previously.A
An acellular pertussis vaccine has been studied in adults and is 63% to 92% effective. A

Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends that physicians consider prophylaxis of household contacts using macrolides at the same doses as for active treatment. However, 2 studies found no symptomatic benefit to prophylaxis of household contacts with erythromycin. The attack rate was higher in unvaccinated contacts than in vaccinated patients (19% vs 0%) but did not differ between those receiving antibiotics and those receiving placebo (18% vs 20%; P = NS). B
Vaccine hesitancy regarding pertussis vaccine by parents is strongly associated with an increased risk of pertussis for their children. A
Vaccination is recommended in pregnancy, with immunization in late 3rd trimester less effective than earlier vaccination based on a systematic review.
Suspect pertussis in patients with prolonged cough accompanied by posttussive vomiting, apnea, or the classic inspiratory "whoop."C
Assume pertussis without need for diagnostic testing in household contacts of confirmed cases with cough illness.C
If pertussis is suspected, order a PCR test and simultaneous culture to confirm the diagnosis. Use a polyester nasopharyngeal swab. C

Pertussis is classically described as having 3 phases, catarrhal, paroxysmal, and convalescent. The catarrhal phase is characterized by cough, coryza, fever (usually not high), and cold-like symptoms and typically lasts 1 to 2 weeks. Patients in the paroxysmal phase have severe, spasmodic cough with the characteristic inspiratory "whoop." The cough is so severe that apnea, vomiting, and conjunctival hemorrhage are not uncommon. Finally, the convalescent phase is characterized by gradual improvement and can last for up to several months.

A study of 141 infants under 1 year of age who were tested for pertussis (13% had confirmed disease) found that pertussis was more common in those who were younger (mean age 55 vs 93 days), were seen in the summer (23% vs 9%), and were less tachypneic (39 vs 47 breaths per minute). In infants under the age of 1 year, apnea was reported in 56%, with the rate declining from 64% between 0 month and 1 month of age to 44% between 10 months and 11 months of age. Cough for at least 2 weeks was seen in 85% of infants, paroxysms in 91%, and the "whoop" in 60%. In infants, the model using cyanosis, cough for more than 1 week, and absence of fever was 89% sensitive for pertussis. In areas of local pertussis outbreaks (where >10% pertussis cultures in region are positive), the model using cyanosis, cough for more than 1 week, and absence of fever was 100% sensitive.

In different reports of pertussis in adolescent populations, 74% to 100% had paroxysmal cough, 77% had difficulty sleeping, 72% had difficulty breathing, 49% to 71% had posttussive vomiting, 31% to 67% had the inspiratory "whoop," 33% had weight loss, and 27% to 86% had apnea. Uncommon complications included pneumonia (2%), hospitalization (0.8%-2.0%), rib fracture (1%), loss of consciousness (1%), and seizure (0.2%-0.3%). In adolescents and adults, presence of inspiratory whoop (LR: 1.9) or posttussive emesis (LR: 1.8) modestly increase the likelihood of pertussis and the absence of paroxysmal cough (LR: 0.52), inspiratory whoop (LR: 0.78), or posttussive emesis (LR: 0.58) modestly decrease the likelihood of pertussis. Among adolescents and adults with prolonged cough illness, 14 studies reported that between 12% and 52% were caused by pertussis.
The WHO criteria for pertussis in adults were highly sensitive (95%) but not specific (15%).
Pertussis is most common during middle-to-late summer but can occur during any month.

A meta-analysis found that the overall clinical assessment of a patient was most useful in ruling in pertussis (LR+ 3.3; LR− 0.63). In children, whooping cough was more diagnostic than in adults (LR+ 2.9 vs 1.9). Other individual signs/symptoms (e.g., posttussive emesis, paroxysmal coughing, sputum production, disturbed sleep by coughing) were minimally useful in ruling in pertussis (LR+ between 1.7 and 0.58).
The recommended sampling technique is to use a polyester nasopharyngeal swab. Insert the swab into the base of the nostril, and leave it in the posterior pharynx for 10 seconds, then withdraw it.

CDC recommends PCR as the preferred test because it is accurate and results can be obtained within 48 hours (compared with 1-2 weeks for culture). Direct fluorescent antigen tests are marginally more specific but much less sensitive, and, although helpful if positive, do not rule out disease if negative. Culture should be ordered simultaneously with PCR to confirm the diagnosis. Use of serology is not recommended.
PCR and culture are recommended only for patients with cough for 2 or more weeks accompanied by posttussive vomiting or characteristic "whoop."

In infants under 1 year of age, an absolute lymphocyte count of greater than 9400 cells/microliter was 89% sensitive and 75% specific (LR+ 3.6; LR− 0.15) for pertussis. In a study of 141 infants with suspected pertussis, only 3% with an absolute lymphocyte count less than 9400 cells/microliter had pertussis.
Suspect pertussis in patients with prolonged cough (>2 weeks) accompanied by posttussive vomiting, apnea, or the classic inspiratory "whoop."
If pertussis is suspected, order the PCR test and culture to confirm the diagnosis.

First-line therapy is azithromycin for infants less than 1 month old; azithromycin, erythromycin, or clarithromycin for children over 1 month old; and azithromycin or clarithromycin for adolescents and adults. B
Sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim is an alternative for patients who cannot tolerate macrolides. B
Treatment for 5 to 7 days with azithromycin or clarithromycin is as good as longer courses of erythromycin. A

Macrolides are traditionally recommended for treatment of pertussis. A systematic review identified 13 studies with 2197 patients; 11 were treatment studies and 2 were prophylaxis studies of household contacts. Only one of the treatment studies was placebo controlled, and it did not report the effect of antibiotics on symptom resolution. Comparisons between different macrolides found only that erythromycin estolate was more effective as measured by clinical cure than erythromycin ethylsuccinate (14% vs 4%; number needed to treat = 10).

CDC treatment recommendations are shown in . Any household contact of a patient with confirmed pertussis who develops a cough illness should be treated as if they had pertussis, though there is insufficient evidence to determine the benefits of prophylactic treatment of pertussis contacts.

Corticosteroids, diphenhydramine, pertussis immunoglobulin, montelukast, and salbutamol have all been studied in small clinical trials with between 9 and 135 patients. There was no clear benefit with any of these interventions, although, given the small size of these studies, a clinical benefit is possible but unproved.
There was no difference in microbiological cure rates between shorter courses (azithromycin for 3-5 days or erythromycin or clarithromycin for 7 days) and longer courses (14 days).

Hospitalization should be strongly considered in infants because of a greater risk of apnea (~60%) and higher likelihood that the patient will need mechanical ventilation (~10%-15%) than in adolescents or adults.
Oxygen, adequate hydration, and nutritional support may be necessary. Approximately 15% of infants require mechanical ventilation.
Among hospitalized infants, 5% to 10% require mechanical ventilation or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. B
Overall mortality is less than 1% in infants and even lower in adolescents and adults. B

In a study at a referral center in Brazil, of 55 children admitted over a 6 year period 17 required PICU admission and 6 (11%) died. Risk factors for a severe course included co-infection with RSV, leukocyte count >40,000/mm on admission, and a mean heart rate during the hospitalization greater than 160 beats/minute.B
